Which infections should we prioritise?

Source: vignettes/prioritise-infections.qmd

The problem

Infection-prevention teams have limited budgets and must decide which hospital-acquired infections to target first. A natural starting point is to count cases. But one infection is not equal to another: a bloodstream infection is far more likely to be fatal than a urinary tract infection. Ranking by case numbers alone can therefore direct resources away from the infections that cause the most harm.

This guide shows how to use haiexplorer to answer one question:

Which hospital-acquired infections cause the most harm, and does the priority order change depending on how harm is measured?

It is written for an infection-prevention manager or analyst who has not used the package before.

Key terms

  • Hospital-acquired infection (HAI): an infection a patient develops during a hospital stay that was not present on admission.
  • Cases: estimated new infections per year.
  • Deaths: estimated deaths caused by the infection per year.
  • DALY (disability-adjusted life year): one year of healthy life lost, counting both early death and time lived in poor health. DALYs allow infections to be compared by the harm they cause, not only by how often they occur.
  • Per 100,000 people: a rate that removes the effect of population size, so Germany and the European average can be compared fairly.
  • Uncertainty range: the range within which the true value lies with 95% probability.

Step 1: Install and load the package

Install the package from GitHub, then load it:

# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("ETC5523-2026/etc5523-assignment-4-vdab0003-design")
library(haiexplorer)

Step 2: Launch the app 

run_app()

The app opens in a new window. It has a sidebar of controls on the left and the results on the right.

Step 3: Use the controls

Control What it does When to use it
Rank infections by Switches between number of cases, deaths and healthy years lost (DALYs) Compare Number of cases with Healthy years lost to see whether the priority order changes
Country Switches between Germany and the European average Check whether priorities differ by setting
Show per 100,000 people Converts totals into rates Turn on when comparing Germany with Europe, because totals depend on population size
Infections to compare Selects which infections are included Focus on the infections your hospital can act on; shares are recalculated for the selection

The Key terms panel at the bottom of the sidebar explains each measure and infection type.

Step 4: Read the outputs

The app shows four linked outputs, all calculated from the same selection:

  1. Summary boxes name the infection with the highest burden, its share of the total, and where it would rank by number of cases. If the last box shows anything other than “1st”, the priority order changes when harm is measured instead of frequency.
  2. The headline states the main finding in one sentence.
  3. The bar chart ranks the infections. The red bar is the largest, and the percentage under each name is its share of the total. The thin line across each bar is the 95% uncertainty range. Where the lines of two infections overlap, the data cannot show with confidence which is larger, so treat those infections as similar priorities.
  4. The table gives the exact estimate, uncertainty range and share for each infection.

If no infections are ticked, the app shows a message asking you to select at least one. If only one is ticked, it explains that there is nothing to rank it against.

Step 5: Interpret the results

The same ranking that powers the app is available as a function, rank_infections(), so the findings can be checked or reused in your own analysis.

The most common infections are not the most harmful

Ranked by number of cases, urinary tract infections are the most frequent in Germany, and bloodstream infections are the least frequent:

rank_infections(hai_burden, measure = "Cases")
#> # A tibble: 5 × 6
#>    rank infection     median  lower  upper share
#>   <int> <chr>          <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1     1 Urinary tract 213525 177470 259600 44.8 
#> 2     2 Pneumonia     106171  83077 134555 22.3 
#> 3     3 Surgical site  93650  74062 116669 19.7 
#> 4     4 C. difficile   36253  24824  50927  7.61
#> 5     5 Bloodstream    26767  17435  40243  5.62

Ranked by healthy years lost, the order changes. Bloodstream infections rise from fifth to third, accounting for about a quarter of the total, because they are much more likely to be fatal:

rank_infections(hai_burden, measure = "DALYs")
#> # A tibble: 5 × 6
#>    rank infection     median lower  upper share
#>   <int> <chr>          <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1     1 Pneumonia      69900 32642 113617 28.5 
#> 2     2 Urinary tract  66373 28197 127111 27.0 
#> 3     3 Bloodstream    59428 30829 100661 24.2 
#> 4     4 Surgical site  28845 22902  35772 11.7 
#> 5     5 C. difficile   20977  1886  47794  8.54

What this means for prioritisation: a prevention plan based only on case counts would place bloodstream infections last, even though they cause almost as much harm as the most common infection. Pneumonia, urinary tract and bloodstream infections should be considered together as the leading priorities when harm is the goal.

Comparing Germany with Europe

Totals cannot be compared directly, because Europe’s population is much larger. Using rates per 100,000 people:

germany <- rank_infections(hai_burden, country = "Germany",
                           scale = "Per 100,000 people")
europe  <- rank_infections(hai_burden, country = "Europe",
                           scale = "Per 100,000 people")

c(Germany = sum(germany$median), Europe = sum(europe$median))
#> Germany  Europe 
#>     304     290

Germany loses slightly more healthy years per 100,000 people than the European average. However, the individual uncertainty ranges are wide, so this difference may not be real. In Europe, pneumonia is clearly the largest burden, while in Germany the top three infections are close.

Limitations

  • The estimates are scaled up from a one-day survey in 2011-12 and may not reflect current conditions.
  • Deaths and DALYs rely on limited evidence about the outcomes of each infection, so their uncertainty ranges are wide. Rankings between infections whose ranges overlap should be treated with caution.
  • The German estimates are based on 46 hospitals, so they are less precise than the European figures.

Data source

Zacher B, Haller S, Willrich N, et al. (2019). Application of a new methodology and R package reveals a high burden of healthcare-associated infections (HAI) in Germany compared to the average in the European Union/ European Economic Area, 2011 to 2012. Eurosurveillance, 24(46), 1900135. Data distributed in the BHAI R package. See ?hai_burden for details of how the data were prepared.
